credit: Hávamál tr. H. A. Bellows (1923); Proverbs, JPS 1917; traditional songs. All public domain.

parts:
Food and clothes
must the farer have,
The man from the mountains come.

If renown he would get,
and again be greeted,
Wisely and well must he act.

At the witless man
the wise shall wink
When among such men he sits.

It is better than wealth
on unknown ways,
And in grief a refuge it gives.

The vulgar man,
when among the wise,
To scorn by his belly is brought.

But the foolish man
his belly's measure
Shall never know aright.

Care-worn he is
when the morning comes,
And his woe is just as it was.

Nought is concealed
that men may say
Among the sons of men.

But wide and straight
is the way to a friend,
Though far away he fare.

A pair of goats
and a patched-up roof
Are better far than begging.

His heart is bleeding
who needs must beg
When food he fain would have.

Gift-givers' friendships
are longest found,
If fair their fates may be.

But men shall mocking
with mockery answer,
And fraud with falsehood meet.

Rich did I feel
when a comrade I found,
For man is man's delight.

With half a loaf
and a half-filled cup
A friend full fast I made.

And man by his speech
is known to men,
And the stupid by their stillness.

The wolf that lies idle
shall win little meat,
Or the sleeping man success.

Tell one thy thoughts,
but beware of two,—
All know what is known to three.

Full oft does the weather
change in a week,
And more in a month's time.

But a noble name
will never die,
If good renown one gets.

If o'er mountains or gulfs
thou fain wouldst go,
Look well to thy food for the way.

For brambles grow
and waving grass
On the rarely trodden road.

None so good is found
that faults he has not,
Nor so wicked that nought he is worth.

Curse not thy guest,
nor show him thy gate,
Deal well with a man in want.
Go to the ant, thou sluggard;
Consider her ways, and be wise;
’Yet a little sleep, a little slumber,
A little folding of the hands to sleep’—
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand;
But the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
A wise son gathereth in summer;
But a son that doeth shamefully sleepeth in harvest.
In the multitude of words there wanteth not transgression;
But he that refraineth his lips is wise.
The beneficent soul shall be made rich,
And he that satisfieth abundantly shall be satisfied also himself.
He that tilleth his ground shall have plenty of bread;
But he that followeth after vain things is void of understanding.
Care in the heart of a man boweth it down;
But a good word maketh it glad.
Hope deferred maketh the heart sick;
But desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise;
But the companion of fools shall smart for it.
A soft answer turneth away wrath;
But a grievous word stirreth up anger.
All the days of the poor are evil;
But he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is,
Than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
A man hath joy in the answer of his mouth;
And a word in due season, how good is it!
Better is a dry morsel and quietness therewith,
Than a house full of feasting with strife.
A friend loveth at all times,
And a brother is born for adversity.
A merry heart is a good medicine;
But a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise;
And he that shutteth his lips is esteemed as a man of understanding.
There are friends that one hath to his own hurt;
But there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep;
And the idle soul shall suffer hunger.
The sluggard will not plow when winter setteth in;
Therefore he shall beg in harvest, and have nothing.
Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty;
Open thine eyes, and thou shalt have bread in plenty.
’It is bad, it is bad’, saith the buyer;
But when he is gone his way, then he boasteth.
He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed;
For he giveth of his bread to the poor.
A word fitly spoken
Is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee,
Lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it.
Let thy foot be seldom in thy neighbour’s house;
Lest he be sated with thee, and hate thee.
The north wind bringeth forth rain,
And a backbiting tongue an angry countenance.
As cold waters to a faint soul,
So is good news from a far country.
The door is turning upon its hinges,
And the sluggard is still upon his bed.
Where no wood is, the fire goeth out;
And where there is no whisperer, contention ceaseth.
Boast not thyself of to-morrow;
For thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
Iron sharpeneth iron;
So a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack;
But he that hideth his eyes shall have many a curse.
The ants are a people not strong,
Yet they provide their food in the summer;

Greensleeves was all my joy,
Greensleeves was my delight,

Greensleeves was my heart of gold,
and who but my Lady Greensleeves.

True Thomas lay on Huntlie bank,
A ferlie he spied wi’ his e’e;

And there he saw a ladye bright
Come riding down by the Eildon Tree.

It's of a pedlar, a pedlar bold
A pedlar bold there chanced to be

He took his pack all on his back
And merrily trudged over the lea
